questions.q: What are the three core elements of an IAM policy statement, per this lesson?
options: Effect, Action, and Resource — read completely literally, with no implied intent
Username, Password, and Region
Bucket, Object, and Key, used only for S3
Cost, Region, and Tag
questions.explain: Every statement is built from Effect (Allow/Deny), Action (the API call), and Resource (the ARN it applies to).

questions.q: Why does an S3 read policy typically need two Resource ARNs — the bucket itself and a /* wildcard?
options: The bucket ARN is needed for bucket-level actions like ListBucket, and the /* wildcard ARN is needed for object-level actions like GetObject on the objects inside it
AWS requires every policy to contain exactly two ARNs regardless of purpose
One ARN is for the AWS Console and the other is only for the CLI
The second ARN is optional decoration with no functional effect
questions.explain: Forgetting the /* object-level ARN while only granting the bucket ARN is one of the most common S3 permission bugs.

questions.q: What distinguishes a resource-based policy from an identity-based policy?
options: A resource-based policy is attached to the resource itself and includes a Principal naming who it grants access to; an identity-based policy is attached to a user, group, or role
Resource-based policies can never grant access across AWS accounts
Identity-based policies are the only type that can include an Effect
There is no real difference between the two
questions.explain: Resource-based policies (like S3 bucket policies) name a Principal because they aren't already attached to the identity being granted access.

questions.q: When multiple policies attached to an identity conflict, what determines the outcome?
options: An explicit Deny anywhere always overrides any Allow, regardless of how many Allow statements exist elsewhere
The Allow statement always wins regardless of any Deny
AWS picks randomly between conflicting statements
Whichever policy was attached most recently always wins
questions.explain: Explicit Deny takes precedence over Allow in AWS's policy evaluation logic, every time.

questions.q: Per this lesson, which policy type is the production standard for granting a data pipeline role its permissions?
options: Customer managed policies — you write the exact scope, version them, and reuse them across roles that need the same access
Inline policies, because they can't be reused across identities
AWS managed policies, because they are always the narrowest option available
There is no standard; any policy type is equally recommended for production
questions.explain: Customer managed policies give exact, versioned, reusable scope — the standard choice for production pipeline roles.
